sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll have three real, working n8n automations running in the cloud — doing actual work for you every day, completely free.

## What is n8n?

n8n (pronounced "n-eight-n") is an open-source workflow automation tool. It lets you connect apps and add AI processing steps using a visual drag-and-drop canvas — no code required for most workflows.

What makes n8n special:
- **Free and open-source** — the core product costs nothing
- **Self-hostable** — you can run it on your own server for total control and privacy
- **Cloud option** — n8n.io offers a managed cloud version with a free tier
- **Native AI nodes** — first-class support for Claude, OpenAI, and other LLMs
- **Code when needed** — for advanced logic, you can drop in a JavaScript Code node

For this lesson you'll use **n8n Cloud** (app.n8n.cloud) — no installation needed. The free tier gives you enough workflows and executions to build everything here.

## The Visual Canvas

Every n8n workflow lives on a canvas. The canvas is made up of **nodes** connected by **arrows** (called edges).

Each node is a step:
- **Trigger nodes** start the workflow (Schedule Trigger, Webhook, Gmail trigger, etc.)
- **Action nodes** do something in an app (send an email, add a spreadsheet row, post to Slack)
- **AI nodes** process text with an LLM (AI Agent, LLM Chain, Summarize, etc.)
- **Code nodes** let you write JavaScript for custom logic
- **HTTP Request nodes** call any API that doesn't have a dedicated node

To connect nodes: hover over the output dot on one node, drag to the input dot on the next node. The arrow you draw is the data flowing between them.

**The AI Agent node** is the one you'll use most. It takes text input, sends it to a model (Claude, OpenAI, etc.) with a system prompt you write, and outputs the model's response. One node handles the entire AI step.

## The Accomplishment Standard

By the end of this workshop you'll have three automations running in production — not demos, but real workflows doing real work in the background while you're doing other things.

All three use n8n Cloud's free tier. All three run on a schedule. All three use an AI step to process data before delivering a result.

sections.title: Build 3 Real n8n Automations
sections.content:
**Setup: Sign up for n8n Cloud**
1. Go to app.n8n.cloud/register
2. Create a free account
3. Your workspace loads with an empty canvas

---

**Automation 1 — Daily AI News Digest (15 min)**

This workflow fetches tech news every morning, has Claude summarize the top stories, and emails the digest to you.

Pipeline: `Schedule Trigger (8am daily)` → `HTTP Request (fetch RSS feed)` → `AI Agent (summarize top 5 stories)` → `Gmail (send digest to yourself)`

Build it:
1. Click **New workflow** on the canvas
2. Add a **Schedule Trigger** node — set it to run daily at 8:00 AM
3. Add an **HTTP Request** node:
   - URL: `https://feeds.feedburner.com/TechCrunch` (or `https://hnrss.org/frontpage` for Hacker News)
   - Method: GET
   - Response format: String
4. Add an **AI Agent** node:
   - Connect your Claude or OpenAI credentials (the node will prompt you to add them)
   - System prompt: `You are a tech news editor. Given an RSS feed, extract the top 5 most interesting stories. For each story: title, one-sentence summary, and why it matters. Flag anything AI-related with a star.`
   - Connect the HTTP Request output to the AI Agent input
5. Add a **Gmail** node:
   - Operation: Send email
   - To: your email address
   - Subject: `Your Daily Tech Digest — {{$now.format('MMMM D')}}`
   - Body: connect to the AI Agent output
6. Click **Test workflow** — run it manually once to verify it works
7. Click **Activate** — the workflow now runs every morning at 8am

**Verify:** Check your inbox within a minute of activating — the manual test should have delivered an email.

---

**Automation 2 — GitHub Stars Tracker (20 min)**

This workflow checks your GitHub stars weekly, finds repos you starred in the last 7 days, has Claude explain each one, and emails you a digest.

Pipeline: `Schedule Trigger (weekly Monday 9am)` → `HTTP Request (GitHub starred repos)` → `Code node (filter by date)` → `AI Agent (explain each repo)` → `Gmail (weekly digest)`

> **API note:** GitHub's starred repos endpoint returns ALL your stars, not just recent ones. The Code node filters by date.

Build it:
1. New workflow → **Schedule Trigger**: every Monday at 9:00 AM
2. **HTTP Request** node:
   - URL: `https://api.github.com/users/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/starred`
   - Method: GET
   - Add header: `Accept: application/vnd.github.star+json` (this includes the `starred_at` timestamp)
3. **Code** node (JavaScript):
```javascript
const sevenDaysAgo = new Date();
sevenDaysAgo.setDate(sevenDaysAgo.getDate() - 7);

const recentStars = $input.all()
  .flatMap(item => item.json)
  .filter(repo => {
    const starredAt = new Date(repo.starred_at);
    return starredAt >= sevenDaysAgo;
  });

return recentStars.map(repo => ({ json: repo }));
```
4. **AI Agent** node:
   - Prompt: `Here is a GitHub repository a developer just starred. Explain in 2-3 sentences: what it does, who it's for, and one reason it might be interesting. Repository data: {{$json}}`
5. **Gmail** node: send a weekly digest of all the AI explanations
6. Activate

---

**Automation 3 — Meeting Prep Brief (25 min)**

This workflow runs every weekday at 7:30am, checks your Google Calendar for today's meetings, and emails you a prep brief.

Pipeline: `Schedule Trigger (weekdays 7:30am)` → `Google Calendar (get today's events)` → `AI Agent (generate prep questions for each meeting)` → `Gmail (send brief by 8am)`

Build it:
1. New workflow → **Schedule Trigger**: weekdays at 7:30 AM
2. **Google Calendar** node:
   - Operation: Get many events
   - Calendar: your primary calendar
   - Time min: today at 00:00
   - Time max: today at 23:59
3. **AI Agent** node:
   - Prompt: `I have the following meeting today: {{$json.summary}} at {{$json.start.dateTime}}. Description: {{$json.description}}. Generate: 3 preparation questions I should think about before this meeting, and any likely action items I should be ready to discuss.`
4. **Gmail** node: send the brief to yourself with subject `Meeting Prep — {{$now.format('dddd MMMM D')}}`
5. Activate

---

**After all 3 are active:**
Document your workflows in your notes file: what each does, when it runs, and how to modify it if needed. You now have a personal AI assistant running 24/7 on the free tier.

sections.title: Workshop A — n8n Installation and First Workflow
sections.content:
Get n8n running and execute your first workflow.

**Step 1 — Install n8n:**
```powershell
npx n8n
```
Or via Docker: `docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 n8nio/n8n`

**Step 2 — Open n8n** at http://localhost:5678 and create an account.

**Step 3 — Create your first workflow:**
- Add a **Schedule Trigger** node (runs every minute for testing)
- Add a **Set** node that creates a variable `message = "Hello from n8n at {{$now}}"`
- Add a **No Operation** node to see the output
- Connect them in order

**Step 4 — Execute the workflow** manually and verify the output in the execution log.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** *"I'm learning n8n. What are the 5 most important node types to understand first? For each, describe what it does and a common use case."*

sections.title: Workshop B — Build a Real n8n Workflow with AI
sections.content:
Build a genuinely useful n8n workflow using AI assistance.

**Step 1 — Choose your automation blueprint** from Lesson 10-1 Workshop D.

**Step 2 — Ask Claude Code** to help you design the n8n workflow:
```
I want to build this workflow in n8n: [describe your automation].

Help me:
1. Which n8n nodes should I use for each step?
2. What should the workflow look like structurally?
3. For any step involving AI processing, how do I use the OpenAI or HTTP Request node to call the Anthropic API?
4. What are the common pitfalls for this type of workflow?
```

**Step 3 — Build the workflow** in n8n following Claude's guidance.

**Step 4 — Test with real data.** Does it work as expected?

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review this n8n workflow I built [describe it]. What failure modes haven't I handled? What happens when [specific API] is down or returns an error?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — n8n Error Handling
sections.content:
Add robust error handling to your n8n workflows.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"What are the most common ways n8n workflows fail in production? For each failure mode, what is the n8n error handling approach?"*

**Step 2 — Identify the failure points** in your workflow from Workshop B.

**Step 3 — Add error handling** to each critical node:
- Add an **Error Trigger** workflow that runs when any workflow fails
- Add retry logic to HTTP Request nodes
- Add condition nodes to handle empty/null responses
- Add a notification step (email or Slack) on failure

**Step 4 — Test error handling** by intentionally breaking part of the workflow (use a wrong API key or URL) and verify the error notification fires.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** *"For a production n8n workflow, what monitoring and alerting should I set up beyond just error notifications?"*

sections.title: Workshop D — n8n + AI Processing Pipeline
sections.content:
Build an n8n workflow that includes AI text processing via the Anthropic API.

**Step 1 — Choose a use case** where AI processing adds value in the middle of a workflow:
- Classify incoming emails by topic
- Summarise long documents before saving to Notion
- Extract structured data from unstructured text
- Generate personalised content based on input data

**Step 2 — Ask Claude Code to generate the Anthropic API call configuration:**
```
Generate an n8n HTTP Request node configuration to call the Anthropic API.
Endpoint: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
Model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
Task: [describe what you want the AI to do with each input]
The input comes from: [previous node output]
```

**Step 3 — Build the workflow** with the AI processing step.

**Step 4 — Test with diverse inputs.** Does the AI consistently produce the right output format?

**Step 5 — Add output validation:** If the AI output doesn't match the expected format, route to a fallback branch.

sections.question: You build an n8n workflow that processes incoming emails with AI. It works in testing but occasionally fails in production. What is the most likely cause?
options: Real-world inputs are more varied than test inputs — the workflow hits edge cases (empty fields, unusual characters, unexpected email formats) that weren't represented in tests
The AI model changes its behaviour over time
sections.explanation: The most common cause of automation failures moving from test to production: real data is messier than test data. Your test emails were well-formed; production emails might have empty subjects, unusual character encodings, very long bodies, attachment-only messages, or formats your workflow didn't anticipate. Fix: test with a diverse sample of real data before going live, and build defensive handling for every field your workflow reads.

sections.question: An n8n workflow sends an automatic response email based on AI classification of incoming messages. What safety mechanism is most important to implement?
options: Rate limiting to prevent too many emails
A human review queue for any message the AI classifies with less than 90% confidence, or for any response that includes personal commitments or sensitive content
Only process emails during business hours
Log all AI classifications for later review
sections.explanation: Automated responses sent under your name or your organisation's name carry real consequences. The critical safety mechanism: identify cases where the automation might respond incorrectly and route those to human review. Low-confidence classifications are one signal; response content is another — any automated response that makes a commitment (scheduling a meeting, approving a request, providing pricing) should require human approval first.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 10-2.** Three real automations are running in the background. Every day your inbox gets smarter — and you did it for free with zero code (except one JavaScript filter). Next: Zapier's approach to the same problem.
